Grant the actions but add a condition on IP address
Grant read-only everywhere and write to one bucket
iam.explanation: Least privilege is about the smallest set of actions on the smallest set of resources. Restricting by region or IP narrows the blast radius but leaves the role able to do far more than it needs within that scope.

iam.text: When should you use an IAM group rather than attaching policies to users directly?
options: When several people share a job function and the same permissions
When a user needs more permissions
iam.explanation: Groups model job function and keep access consistent: add or remove the person, not the policy. Attaching to individuals means access drifts and you can no longer answer who has what by looking at one place.

iam.text: What does an SCP do that an IAM policy does not?
options: It sets the maximum permissions available to an account in an organisation, bounding what its IAM policies can grant
It applies only to root users
iam.explanation: SCPs are an allow-list ceiling applied at the account level. An identity policy can only ever narrow that ceiling, never widen it, which is what makes them useful for guardrails.

iam.text: Why can a role trust policy cause an unexpected privilege escalation path?
options: If a low-privilege principal is allowed to assume a high-privilege role, it inherits that role's permissions
Trust policies are evaluated after identity policies, so they add permissions
A trust policy grants the role to every account
Trust policies cannot be edited by account admins
iam.explanation: This is the classic confused-deputy pattern: a principal with AssumeRole on something powerful can effectively become that principal. Audit who can assume which roles, and use aws:ExternalId for third-party access.

iam.text: What is the practical effect of removing all inline policies but leaving managed policies attached?
options: The principal keeps the permissions from its managed policies
iam.explanation: Inline and managed policies are additive. Cleaning up inline policies while leaving managed ones attached is a common source of surprise access, so review both lists together.

iam.text: Why does using the AWS managed AdministratorAccess policy for a human user tend to be flagged in audits?
options: It cannot be scoped down and gives unrestricted access to every service including billing and IAM
It is slower than a custom policy
It is not available in all regions
iam.explanation: It is a valid choice for a break-glass account but a poor default: audits cannot distinguish real need from convenience, and it grants access to IAM and billing, the two things that make an account unrecoverable.

iam.text: What does sts:TagSession do during role assumption?
options: Passes session tags that appear in CloudTrail, letting you trace who assumed the role
iam.explanation: Session tags are the cleanest way to attribute an assumed role back to a person in an audit trail, especially when the principal itself is just a role.

iam.text: Which is a real risk of using a single long-lived IAM user for automation?
options: The key can leak and there is no automatic rotation, and it cannot be tied to a session
It cannot be used with the CLI
It is limited to one region
iam.explanation: Long-lived keys are a standing liability: anyone who obtains one has that access until someone notices. IAM roles with short-lived credentials remove both the rotation problem and the attribution problem.

interview-prep.text: Which structure is most effective when describing a production incident?
options: STAR, emphasising your specific actions and a measurable result
A chronological account of everything that happened
A technical deep dive on the root cause only
A blame-focused account of other teams"
interview-prep.explanation: STAR gives the interviewer a predictable structure so they can follow your decision points. Spend the most time on Action, since that is what they assess, and close with a quantified Result and what you changed afterwards. A chronological recount buries the decisions, and technical-only leaves them unable to judge how you operate under pressure.

interview-prep.text: What makes a strong answer to 'tell me about a time you disagreed with a decision'?
options: You raised the concern with evidence, respected the outcome, and committed to measuring it
You disagreed, were overruled, and quietly did it your own way
You waited until after it shipped to object
You escalated to your manager straight away"
interview-prep.explanation: Interviewers are assessing whether you raise concerns with evidence and can commit once a decision is made. Quietly doing it your own way is far worse than disagreeing, and immediate escalation reads as political. The follow-up they listen for is what you did next: helped measure the outcome, or kept arguing.

interview-prep.text: How should you open a system design round?
options: Clarify requirements, scale, constraints and success criteria before proposing anything
Propose your preferred architecture immediately to show expertise
Start with the database choice since it is hardest
Ask what stack they use and design around it"
interview-prep.explanation: Requirements and constraints drive every later choice, and asking them signals you can size a system rather than guess. Saying your assumptions out loud lets the interviewer correct you early. Jumping to an architecture risks building the wrong system very convincingly.

interview-prep.text: What is a good answer to 'where do you see yourself in three years'?
options: A direction tied to the role, without demanding a specific title
A specific job title you will have reached
That you want to move into management
That you are unsure and open to anything"
interview-prep.explanation: A direction that builds on the role reads as committed and coachable, whereas demanding a title or declaring management ambition narrows you needlessly. Unsure and open suggests no drive. The interviewer wants to see your next step is contiguous with what they offer, so tie it to their actual problems.

interview-prep.text: Why do interviewers ask about a failure you caused?
options: To see how you surface it, communicate it, and fix the class of problem rather than the instance
To catch candidates with poor judgement
Because they need someone to blame internally
To see if you can hide a mistake"
interview-prep.explanation: Everyone causes incidents; what separates senior engineers is the response. A good answer shows you noticed quickly, told stakeholders before they noticed, fixed the immediate problem, then made the failure class less likely through a review, alert or test. Listen for 'we' rather than 'they', and a systemic fix rather than a heroics story.

interview-prep.text: What is the most credible first step to demonstrate DevOps capability when moving from development?
options: Owning one production service end to end, including pipeline, monitoring, alerts and on-call
interview-prep.explanation: Interviewers want evidence you have run systems, not studied them. Owning one service with real on-call responsibility and documented reliability outcomes is a far stronger signal than certifications, which prove attendance. Open-source work is also strong but slower to land.

interview-prep.text: How should you answer about a gap such as never running multi-region failover?
options: State the gap honestly, describe the closest adjacent experience, and outline how you would approach it
Avoid the question and highlight another strength
Claim you have done it but keep it vague
Say you would need training and stop there"
interview-prep.explanation: Honesty plus a clear approach beats both a dodge and an overclaim. Interviewers assess judgement, and reasoning about an unsolved problem is a good signal. Overclaiming is the worst outcome, easy to probe and expensive if uncovered, and vagueness reads as evasive.

interview-prep.text: Which question signals genuine interest in a DevOps role?
options: How does the team handle a deployment when the on-call engineer is already in an incident?
How many people are on the team?
interview-prep.explanation: This is specific, shows you already understand that reliability work overlaps incident response, and invites a real answer about process and tooling. The stack question gets you a list; the on-call question gets you the operating philosophy, which is what you are actually deciding on.

interview-prep.text: What is the most common mistake candidates make when describing system design trade-offs?
options: Presenting one architecture with no alternatives or reasoning, so there is nothing to discuss
interview-prep.explanation: Design interviews are a conversation about trade-offs. Presenting a single design with no alternatives removes the discussion the interviewer is trying to have, and makes it impossible to tell whether you chose deliberately or by default. Offering two options with the trade-off between them demonstrates judgement directly.

interview-prep.text: In a STAR answer, what proportion of your time should go to describing your own actions?
options: The majority, because that is what the interviewer is assessing
As little as possible, to focus on the team
None, since actions are usually obvious"
interview-prep.explanation: Situation and Task are usually a sentence or two each. Action and Result take the remaining time, and Result should be quantified. Spending most of the answer on setup context is the most common way candidates lose an otherwise strong interview.

interview-prep.text: You are asked to explain a production outage you did not cause. What is the strongest opening?
options: State what you observed, what you ruled out, and what you changed, with the evidence
Describe how the previous team should have prevented it
Give your opinion on the architecture first
interview-prep.explanation: Interviewers are testing how you reason under pressure. Leading with observations, eliminations and evidence demonstrates the process; leading with blame or architecture opinion does not, whatever the merits.

interview-prep.text: What is the difference between explaining a tool and explaining a decision?
options: A decision includes the constraints and alternatives considered; a tool description does not
interview-prep.explanation: Interviewers have heard the tool description many times. What distinguishes a strong candidate is naming the constraint that forced the choice, the alternatives rejected, and the trade-off accepted. That is the part they cannot get from documentation.

interview-prep.text: When you do not know the answer to a technical question, what is the best response?
options: Say what you do not know, describe how you would find out, and answer the part you are confident about
Guess confidently, because admitting gaps looks weak
Change the subject to something you know
Say you would ask a colleague rather than answering
interview-prep.explanation: Interviewers are assessing reasoning, not recall. Naming the exact command, log or document you would check demonstrates that you know how to find answers, which is the actual job requirement.

interview-prep.text: How should you answer a question about a weakness or a gap in your experience?
options: Name a real gap, show what you are doing to close it, and give an example of learning quickly
Pick a weakness that sounds like a strength
interview-prep.explanation: A gap with a plan and evidence of self-teaching is credible. A disguised strength reads as evasive, and claiming none is usually challenged by the first technical question.

interview-prep.text: In a system design question, when should you start discussing trade-offs?
options: After clarifying requirements and scale, before proposing technology
At the end, as a summary
interview-prep.explanation: Trade-offs before requirements are meaningless because you do not know what matters yet. Once read and write throughput or consistency needs are stated, the constraints become concrete and trade-offs can be discussed meaningfully.

interview-prep.text: What is the most useful thing to do when a system design interview goes off script?
options: State the assumption you are making and ask whether it matches what they had in mind
Follow the question silently and hope it works out
Answer with a generic architecture diagram
interview-prep.explanation: Interviews are often deliberately open-ended. Verbalising an assumption lets the interviewer correct it early, which is exactly the communication skill the interview is testing.

interview-prep.text: How should you describe the impact of a project quantitatively when you lack formal metrics?
options: Give a before-and-after comparison with the measurement method you used, and be explicit about its limits
Describe the effort rather than the result
Say the metrics were not available
interview-prep.explanation: Interviewers can tell the difference between a precise number and a bounded estimate. Stating the method and its limits is more credible than a confident figure, and it demonstrates measurement discipline.

interview-prep.text: What should you ask at the end of an interview?
options: How the team decides success in the role, and what a recent failure taught
interview-prep.explanation: Asking how success is measured tells you what the role actually is, which is often more informative than the job description. Questions about specific recent failures usually produce candid, revealing answers.

interview-prep.text: Why is describing what you personally did, rather than what the team did, important?
options: Interviews assess individual capability, and vague team framing reads as evasion
interview-prep.explanation: Use we for context but be precise about your own contribution. An interviewer who cannot separate your contribution may assume the weakest part of it was yours.

interview-prep.text: What is a reasonable way to handle a disagreement with a senior engineer in a technical discussion?
options: Present the concern with evidence, commit to their decision if it is made, and offer to test your hypothesis
interview-prep.explanation: This is the classic probe for whether someone can raise a concern without being obstructive. Committing to the decision once made, and offering a cheap way to verify, is what separates a professional from an obstacle.

interview-prep.text: How much implementation detail should you give when asked to whiteboard a pipeline?
options: Enough to show the stages, their inputs and outputs, and the failure handling
Every line of the config file
interview-prep.explanation: Interviewers are looking for whether you know what each stage needs and how failures flow. Reading out configuration line by line burns the time that should go to reasoning.

interview-prep.text: What is the best way to prepare for a behavioural question about a difficult decision?
options: Prepare the situation, your options, what you chose, what you would change, and the measured outcome
interview-prep.explanation: Interviewers follow up on the decision and the reflection, not the narrative. Having the options and the retrospective ready is what makes the answer sound considered rather than rehearsed.

kubernetes.text: What is the purpose of a Kubernetes readiness probe?
options: Restarts the container when it fails
Removes the pod from Service endpoints while keeping it running
Schedules the pod onto a node"
kubernetes.explanation: Readiness controls traffic, not liveness. Failing readiness takes the pod out of Service endpoints so no new requests arrive, but the container keeps running and can recover. That is the right probe for slow warm-up or a temporarily unavailable dependency.

kubernetes.text: What does a liveness probe failure trigger?
options: The pod is removed from Service endpoints
The container is restarted by the kubelet
The pod is rescheduled to another node
kubernetes.explanation: A failed liveness probe causes the kubelet to kill the container, which then restarts under the pod's restartPolicy. This is why liveness must only check the process itself: wiring it to a database turns a downstream outage into a crash loop.

kubernetes.text: Which QoS class results when a pod sets equal requests and limits for CPU and memory on every container?
options: The default, which cannot be set"
kubernetes.explanation: Guaranteed requires equal requests and limits for both CPU and memory on all containers. Those pods are the last evicted under node pressure. BestEffort (nothing set) is evicted first, and Burstable covers everything between.

kubernetes.text: Why do you set resource requests rather than relying on limits?
options: Requests drive scheduling; limits are only a runtime ceiling
Requests are optional and limits are mandatory
Limits are used by the scheduler and requests are not
kubernetes.explanation: The scheduler places pods using requests, which reserve capacity so nodes are not oversubscribed. Limits are enforced afterwards by the kubelet, and CPU over-limit behaviour is throttling rather than termination. Under-requesting CPU causes throttling and eviction even when the node looks half empty.

kubernetes.text: What does the container exit code 137 usually indicate?
options: OOM kill from exceeding the memory limit
kubernetes.explanation: 137 is 128 plus signal 9 (SIGKILL), most often the cgroup OOM killer because the container exceeded its memory limit. 143 is the graceful equivalent (SIGTERM). A failed liveness probe also produces a kill, so check the pod events and reason to distinguish them.

kubernetes.text: When should you use a startup probe instead of a long initialDelaySeconds on liveness?
options: When the app needs a long, variable warm-up and you do not want liveness running during boot
When the app never becomes ready
When there is more than one container per pod
kubernetes.explanation: A startup probe gates liveness and readiness: they do not begin until it succeeds. That lets you keep the normal, aggressive liveness settings for the lifetime of the process instead of inflating the delay and weakening the check.

kubernetes.text: What does the Kubernetes scheduler use when placing a pod?
kubernetes.explanation: Scheduling is driven by requests so nodes are never oversubscribed at the CPU and memory level. This is why a pod can stay Pending with insufficient cpu even when the node's actual usage looks low: existing requests have reserved the capacity.

kubernetes.text: Why can pods be evicted from a node even though the cluster has spare capacity elsewhere?
options: Eviction happens per node on memory or disk pressure, not across the cluster
Eviction only happens when the cluster is full
Pods are evicted during upgrades only
Eviction requires a PodDisruptionBudget to be unset"
kubernetes.explanation: The kubelet evicts pods on its own node when that node runs out of memory or ephemeral storage. Adding nodes elsewhere does not help that node. A pod eviction storm almost always means requests are misconfigured relative to real usage.

kubernetes.text: What is the function of a PodDisruptionBudget?
options: Constrains voluntary disruptions such as node drains during upgrades
Limits how many pods a Deployment can create
Prevents a pod from being scheduled on a specific node
kubernetes.explanation: A PDB sets a floor on available replicas during voluntary disruption, so drains and cluster upgrades proceed without taking a service below its minimum. It does not protect against involuntary failures like a crash or a node failure.

kubernetes.text: Which Service type exposes a service outside the VPC using a cloud provider load balancer?
kubernetes.explanation: LoadBalancer provisions an external load balancer and exposes the Service outside the cluster. NodePort opens a port on every node IP, bypassing the cloud load balancer. ClusterIP is internal only.

kubernetes.text: What is the benefit of using a NetworkPolicy?
options: It restricts traffic between pods by label, providing segmentation within a namespace
It replaces the Kubernetes Service object
It replaces security groups for all traffic
kubernetes.explanation: A NetworkPolicy restricts pod-to-pod traffic by pod selector, namespace selector and port. Without one, all pods in a namespace can talk to all others. Note that most CNIs require the feature to be enabled explicitly.

kubernetes.text: How does a pod obtain an IP address in a typical cluster?
options: The CNI plugin on the node assigns it during pod sandbox creation
The API server allocates it when the pod is created
kube-proxy assigns it after the Service is created
kubernetes.explanation: The kubelet asks the CNI plugin to create the pod's network sandbox, and the plugin assigns the address. In EKS the AWS VPC CNI attaches an ENI, which is why pods get routable private IPs. The pod shows as Pending until this completes.

kubernetes.text: What does the imagePullPolicy of IfNotPresent do?
options: Pulls the image only if it is not already present on the node
Never pulls, failing if the image is absent
kubernetes.explanation: IfNotPresent uses the cached image when present, which speeds up restarts on a warm node. Because a tag like latest is only pulled once under this policy, that is why mutable tags combined with IfNotPresent can serve stale code.

kubernetes.text: Why should ConfigMap values sourced through env vars require a pod restart to change?
options: env values are resolved once at container start, unlike mounted files
env vars cannot be updated by the kubelet at all
ConfigMaps mounted as env are read-only permanently
The API server caches env values"
kubernetes.explanation: Values referenced through env or envFrom are injected into the container's environment at start and never change. Mounted ConfigMap volumes are synced by the kubelet about once a minute and do update in place, so the two mechanisms behave differently and it matters which one your app uses.

kubernetes.text: What happens to a pod with a CrashLoopBackOff state?
options: The container is repeatedly restarted with increasing backoff
The pod is deleted and recreated immediately
The pod is rescheduled to another node
kubernetes.explanation: CrashLoopBackOff means the container keeps exiting and the kubelet backs off between restarts, from 10 seconds up to a five-minute cap. The container's current logs are usually empty, so the error is in the previous instance's logs.

kubernetes.text: How do you make a Deployment rollout back to the previous ReplicaSet quickly?
options: Change the image tag to empty"
kubernetes.explanation: rollout undo reverts the Deployment's pod template, and Kubernetes then scales the previous ReplicaSet back up. Deleting the ReplicaSet leaves the Deployment to create fresh pods, which is not a rollback and loses the known-good spec.

kubernetes.text: What is the effect of setting a Deployment's strategy to Recreate?
options: All existing pods are killed before new ones start, causing downtime
New pods start before old ones are removed, with no downtime
Only one pod is replaced at a time
kubernetes.explanation: Recreate scales the old ReplicaSet to zero before scaling the new one up, which is a deliberate choice for workloads that cannot run two versions at once, such as those with exclusive resource claims. The default RollingUpdate avoids downtime.

kubernetes.text: Why is a StatefulSet used instead of a Deployment for a database with persistent storage?
options: It gives each pod a stable identity and its own persistent volume claim
kubernetes.explanation: A StatefulSet provides stable network identities and per-pod persistent volume claims that follow the pod across rescheduling, which is what a database needs. Deployments give interchangeable pods, which is wrong for stateful workloads.

kubernetes.text: What does the Kubernetes scheduler's taint and toleration mechanism do?
options: Taints repel pods that do not tolerate them, reserving nodes for specific workloads
Taints label pods for the scheduler to group
Tolerations set resource limits on a pod
Taints restrict which namespaces a node accepts pods from"
kubernetes.explanation: A taint on a node repels pods lacking a matching toleration, keeping general workloads off specialised nodes such as GPU or control-plane nodes. Tolerations allow specific pods in; they do not grant scheduling by themselves, since the scheduler still needs to fit the pod.

kubernetes.text: What is the purpose of a ResourceQuota in a namespace?
options: It caps the total compute and object resources a namespace can consume
It assigns pods to specific nodes
It limits the number of replicas per Deployment"
kubernetes.explanation: A ResourceQuota aggregates limits across a namespace, for example CPU, memory and object counts, which prevents one team from consuming the cluster. A LimitRange sets the defaults and per-object bounds for individual pods and containers.

kubernetes.text: Which probe configuration prevents traffic to an application that depends on a slow-starting cache?
options: A readiness probe with an appropriate initialDelaySeconds, and no liveness probe tied to the cache
A liveness probe pointed at the cache
kubernetes.explanation: Readiness alone is correct: the pod stays out of endpoints until the cache warms, then joins. Tying liveness to the cache is the classic mistake that converts a slow cache into a container restart loop.

kubernetes.text: What does setting a container's request equal to its limit achieve for CPU?
options: Guaranteed CPU shares under contention, with throttling once the quota is exceeded
Guaranteed CPU with no throttling possible
kubernetes.explanation: An equal request and limit places the pod in the Guaranteed QoS class, so under node contention it gets reserved shares. Over the limit, the cgroup throttles the container, so latency rises even though the container keeps running. Burst credits only exist on burstable instances like T2.

kubernetes.text: Which command reveals why a pod could not be scheduled?
options: kubectl describe pod <name>, which lists scheduling events
kubernetes.explanation: describe includes the Events section, which carries messages such as insufficient cpu or untolerated taint with the specific numbers. get and logs will not show scheduling failures, and top only reports running workloads.

kubernetes.text: What happens when a pod references a ConfigMap key that does not exist, without the optional flag?
options: The pod starts with an empty value
The kubelet creates an empty ConfigMap
The pod is deleted and retried forever"
kubernetes.explanation: Without optional: true, the kubelet cannot build the container's config and reports CreateContainerConfigError, retrying until the key appears. With optional: true the pod starts and the value is simply absent, which is the safer choice for non-critical settings.

kubernetes.text: How does the HPA compute desired replicas from a CPU utilisation target?
options: It scales the ratio of current utilisation to the target, applied to current replicas
It adds one pod whenever utilisation exceeds the target
It uses memory limits instead of CPU requests
It doubles replicas when utilisation doubles"
kubernetes.explanation: The formula is desired = ceil(currentReplicas x currentUtilisation / targetUtilisation), averaged across pods and clamped by min and max. Crucially utilisation is measured against each pod's CPU request, so wrong requests make the HPA misbehave.

kubernetes.text: What is the difference between a Deployment and a ReplicaSet?
options: A Deployment manages ReplicaSets to provide declarative updates and rollbacks
kubernetes.explanation: The ReplicaSet keeps a number of pods running. The Deployment sits above it and manages ReplicaSets, which is what gives you declarative updates, controlled rollout and rollback. You rarely write ReplicaSets by hand.

kubernetes.text: What does a Pod's phase of Unknown indicate?
options: The node's kubelet stopped reporting, so the control plane cannot determine pod state
The pod image failed to pull
kubernetes.explanation: Unknown means communication with the kubelet was lost, which points at the node or the network path rather than the application. Check node status and the kubelet, not the workload.

kubernetes.text: Which statement about Secrets in Kubernetes is accurate?
options: They are base64-encoded, not encrypted, unless you configure at-rest encryption
They are encrypted at rest by default
They are only readable by the namespace admin
They are stored in etcd unencrypted but protected by RBAC alone"
kubernetes.explanation: Secret data is base64-encoded, which is encoding rather than encryption. At-rest encryption needs an EncryptionConfiguration or an external KMS provider, and scoping access is down to RBAC, so treat Secret RBAC as the primary control.

kubernetes.text: What is the effect of removing a node selector from a running Deployment without changing the image?
options: Nothing happens until pods are recreated, then new pods may schedule elsewhere
kubernetes.explanation: Pods are not rescheduled just because a template field changed. Existing pods keep running until something replaces them, at which point the new spec applies and they may land on different nodes. That delay surprises people expecting a change to take effect immediately.

kubernetes.text: When is an initContainer required rather than a startup script?
options: When setup must complete successfully before the main containers start, or when setup needs different resources or security context
When the app needs environment variables
When the pod needs a Service"
kubernetes.explanation: An initContainer runs to completion in order before the main containers start, and a failure blocks the pod. This is the right pattern for migrations or fetching secrets, and it also allows setup to use a different image, resources or security context than the app.

kubernetes.text: What does setting a Service's sessionAffinity to ClientIP require to work effectively?
options: The client IP must be preserved end to end, which an external load balancer may not do
The pods must run on one node
The Service must use a NodePort"
kubernetes.explanation: ClientIP affinity keys on the source IP, so it only works if that IP survives the whole path. A cloud load balancer that terminates and re-originates can change it, making affinity unreliable unless the LB preserves the address.

kubernetes.text: What is the effect of a Pod having activeDeadlineSeconds?
options: The kubelet terminates it after the deadline and the controller replaces it
It becomes read-only after the deadline
It limits how long the container may run in total across retries"
kubernetes.explanation: activeDeadlineSeconds is a hard limit on the pod's total lifetime, including retries, enforced with a Terminating state and SIGTERM followed by SIGKILL. It is a safety net for jobs that can hang forever, not a graceful timeout.

kubernetes.text: Which pattern reduces a Deployment's blast radius without changing the code?
options: Spread replicas across nodes with topologySpreadConstraints or podAntiAffinity
kubernetes.explanation: Topology spread constraints and anti-affinity distribute replicas so a single node loss cannot take out every replica. Raising replica count helps capacity but can put them all on one node, so it does not address correlated failure.

kubernetes.text: What does kube-proxy do?
options: Programs node networking rules so Service virtual IPs reach the backing pods
kubernetes.explanation: kube-proxy watches Services and EndpointSlices and programs iptables or IPVS rules so the ClusterIP is load balanced to pod IPs. IP assignment is the CNI's job and DNS is CoreDNS's, which are separate components often confused with it.

kubernetes.text: Which command streams logs from all pods in a deployment, including previous crashed instances?
kubernetes.explanation: --all-pods=true reads logs from every pod in the deployment, which matters when the container is crash looping and the current instance has produced nothing. --prefix labels which pod each line came from.

linux.text: What does a process state of D mean?
options: Uninterruptible disk sleep, waiting on I/O
linux.explanation: D is uninterruptible sleep, usually waiting on storage or NFS. It cannot be killed until the I/O completes, which is why D-state processes survive kill -9. A flood of D-state processes pointing at an unresponsive NFS mount is a classic cause of a wedged host.

linux.text: Which signal cannot be caught or ignored?
linux.explanation: SIGKILL and SIGSTOP are the only two the kernel does not let a process intercept. SIGKILL is used when termination must be guaranteed, but it leaves no chance to clean up, so prefer SIGTERM and escalate only if needed.

linux.text: What does the setgid bit on a directory do?
options: New files inherit the directory's group rather than the creator's primary group
Makes new files inherit the directory's permissions
linux.explanation: chmod g+s on a directory makes new files and subdirectories take the directory's group, which is how shared project directories let a whole team edit files. On a regular file, setgid means executable as the group owner, which is what sudo uses.

linux.text: Why can a filesystem report 'No space left on device' while df -h shows free space?
options: Inodes are exhausted, which df -i reveals
df is reporting in different units
The root reserve blocks the write"
linux.explanation: df -h measures data blocks and df -i measures inodes, and they fill at different rates. A directory holding hundreds of thousands of tiny files exhausts inodes while the block count stays low. Removing the small files frees inodes immediately.

linux.text: What does kill -9 send?
options: SIGKILL, which the kernel enforces immediately
SIGTERM with a nine second delay
linux.explanation: kill sends SIGTERM (15), which a well-behaved service uses to drain and flush before exiting. kill -9 sends SIGKILL (9), enforced at once, so temp files and half-written state are left behind. In systemd, systemctl stop sends SIGTERM and only escalates after TimeoutStopSec.

linux.text: Should you be concerned when free memory on a Linux host is near zero?
options: No; free memory is used for page cache, so check available memory and swap activity
Yes, it indicates a memory leak
No, because Linux ignores unused RAM"
linux.explanation: Linux deliberately fills spare RAM with page cache and reclaims it under pressure, so low free with healthy available is normal and good. The signals that matter are available dropping, swap being used, and si/so in vmstat showing active swapping. In containers, watch the cgroup limit rather than the host.

linux.text: Which command shows which process holds a TCP port?
linux.explanation: ss -tlnp lists listening sockets with the process name and PID, and needs root to see other users' processes. lsof -i :8080 is the classic equivalent, and netstat -tlnp is the fallback on minimal images that lack ss.

linux.text: What does '?' in the TTY column of ps output indicate?
options: The process has no controlling terminal
The process runs in a different session"
linux.explanation: No controlling terminal is typical of daemons and kernel threads. It is a quick way to spot user-initiated processes in a list otherwise dominated by services.

linux.text: Why does a container get exit code 137 even though the host has free memory?
options: It exceeded its cgroup memory limit and was OOM-killed
The host ran out of memory
linux.explanation: Containers are bounded by cgroup limits independent of host capacity, so a process can be killed with the host showing plenty free. Check docker stats for usage against the container's limit, and set the limit explicitly rather than inheriting an unknown one.

linux.text: What does status=203/EXEC mean in a systemd unit failure?
options: The ExecStart command could not be executed
linux.explanation: 203/EXEC specifically means systemd could not execute the binary. Common causes: a wrong absolute path, CRLF line endings from a file edited on Windows, a missing shebang, or a mount with noexec. systemctl status plus journalctl -u gives the precise message.

linux.text: Which command shows live HTTP headers during a request?
linux.explanation: -A prints the payload as ASCII so HTTP headers are readable. -X shows hex and ASCII, useful for binary content. Always add -nn to avoid slow reverse lookups and -i any to capture across interfaces.

linux.text: How do you find which files a running process has open?
linux.explanation: lsof -p lists open file descriptors, including sockets and the current working directory, which often spots a process writing somewhere unexpected. strace -p attaches a syscall tracer and shows exactly which paths it tries to open, which pinpoints the cause when lsof only shows the symptom.

linux.text: Why does a union filesystem mean deleting a large file in a RUN step does not shrink an image?
options: Each RUN is a new layer and image size sums all layers, including the deleted data
rm does not work inside images
The base image layer is compressed
linux.explanation: Layers are additive and never shrink, so apt lists downloaded in layer N persist even after deletion in N+1. The fix is combining install and cleanup in one RUN with &&, or using multi-stage builds.

linux.text: What does vmstat show that top does not?
options: Block I/O, context switches and swap in/out activity
linux.explanation: vmstat gives the system-level view: si and so show active swapping, bi and bo show block I/O, and the context switch rate shows scheduler pressure. That is what distinguishes a CPU problem from an I/O or memory-thrash problem.

linux.text: What is the difference between a soft and a hard link to a file?
options: A soft link is a path that points at a name; a hard link is another directory entry for the same inode
A hard link can cross filesystems, a soft link cannot
A soft link cannot point at directories"
linux.explanation: A hard link shares the inode, so deleting the original does not free the data while any hard link remains, but it cannot cross filesystems and cannot point at a directory. A symlink stores a path, survives the target being renamed, and can cross filesystems, but breaks if the target is deleted.

linux.text: Why does a running system ignore changes made to /etc/fstab until a reboot or mount -a?
options: The kernel and systemd cache the mount table; mount -a applies it without rebooting
fstab is only read at boot by design
It does; a reload is always required first"
linux.explanation: fstab is read at boot and by systemd at daemon-reload. mount -a applies any new or changed entries immediately, and systemctl daemon-reload picks up unit changes. Rebooting is a common but unnecessary way to apply a mount change.

linux.text: What does a zombie process indicate?
options: Its parent has not reaped it after it exited
The process is sleeping on I/O
The process is out of memory"
linux.explanation: A zombie has already exited and is only holding a PID slot, because the parent has not called wait(). The fix is in the parent, typically a process that does not reap children, so restarting the parent resolves it. A handful is harmless; thousands means a PID leak.

linux.text: Which command shows the open file descriptor limit for a process?
linux.explanation: /proc/<pid>/limits shows the actual limits in force for that process, including open files. ulimit -a shows the current shell's limits, which may not match what a running daemon inherited. ls -l /proc/<pid>/fd lists descriptors but not the limits themselves.

linux.text: What does strace attach to and show?
options: System calls made by a process, which pinpoints where a failure originates
linux.explanation: strace shows syscalls such as open, read and connect, which is how you find out a process is trying to open a path that does not exist or retrying a connection that is refused. Attach with -p and filter with -e to keep the output readable.

linux.text: Why can a systemd unit fail with 'Failed to start ... because the control process exited'?
options: ExecStart ran but the process exited non-zero, often after failing its own startup checks
The unit file has a syntax error
linux.explanation: That message means the process started and then exited non-zero, as opposed to 203/EXEC which means it could not start at all. journalctl -u <unit> -e shows the process's own error output, which is usually the actual cause.

linux.text: What is checked first when diagnosing high load average with low CPU utilisation across all cores?
options: Processes blocked in uninterruptible I/O wait, shown as D state
The load average calculation itself is wrong
The number of running processes is always accurate"
linux.explanation: Load average counts runnable and uninterruptible tasks, so it can be high while CPU sits idle. That combination almost always means storage or NFS latency, and the processes in D state are the ones to look at.

linux.text: How do environment variables get into a systemd service?
options: From Environment= directives in the unit file or a drop-in, not from your interactive shell
Inherited automatically from the shell that ran systemctl
linux.explanation: Services do not inherit the interactive environment, which is the usual reason a variable works in your shell but is empty in the service. Use Environment= or EnvironmentFile= in a drop-in under /etc/systemd/system/<unit>.d/, then systemctl daemon-reload.

linux.text: What does ss -s or netstat -s summarise?
options: Socket statistics, including errors and retransmits
linux.explanation: Summarised socket counters show cumulative errors, resets and retransmits, which helps distinguish a network problem from an application problem quickly. Compare the deltas over an interval rather than the totals, which are usually high on a long-running host.

linux.text: Why does deleting an open file not free its disk space immediately?
options: The inode stays allocated until the last file descriptor is closed
The file is moved to a temp directory
linux.explanation: The directory entry is removed but the inode and blocks are held until the last open descriptor closes. This is why you can free space on a running service by deleting a large file the service is still writing to, and why the space reappears if the service reopens it.

linux.text: What does the -9 flag's absence in kill -TERM imply about process shutdown?
options: The process is given time to handle the signal and clean up before the kernel acts
The kernel kills it immediately regardless
The signal is sent to the process group
The process is suspended rather than terminated"
linux.explanation: SIGTERM is a request: a well-written process closes listeners, finishes in-flight work and exits. Giving it a grace period before SIGKILL is what prevents dropped connections and half-written state during a restart.

linux.text: Which command shows which filesystem a given file is on?
linux.explanation: df reports usage per filesystem, so it answers which filesystem and how full. du reports the space a file or directory occupies, which is a different question. For a path that is not a mount point, df walks up to the containing filesystem.

linux.text: What is the cause of 'cannot allocate memory' when free reports plenty available?
options: A limit on virtual address space or a process count limit, not physical memory
The page cache is too large
The kernel version is too old"
linux.explanation: Allocation failures often come from limits rather than exhaustion: RLIMIT_AS, a cgroup memory limit, or overcommit settings. Check /proc/<pid>/limits and the cgroup limit for the service rather than trusting free.

linux.text: What does iostat -x 1 most directly tell you?
options: Per-device utilisation, await and queue depth, which separates slow IOPS from slow latency
linux.explanation: -x adds the extended fields: %util, await and aqu-sz. High util with low await points at saturation; low util with high await points at slow media or high queue depth elsewhere. Missing await is why plain iostat often misleads.

linux.text: When should you use update-alternatives or a version manager rather than editing PATH?
options: When multiple versions of the same tool are installed and you need to switch the default
When a binary is not on PATH at all
When the shell is not bash"
linux.explanation: update-alternatives manages symlinks for system-wide defaults on Debian-family systems, which survives package upgrades. Editing PATH in a profile works per user but does not help daemons, which do not read your shell profile.

linux.text: What does the exit status 127 from a shell script indicate?
linux.explanation: 127 conventionally means the command could not be found, and 126 means found but not executable, commonly a permission or noexec problem. Both are shell conventions rather than kernel guarantees, but they are reliable enough to branch on in scripts.

monitoring.text: What are the three Prometheus metric types and when is each used?
options: Counter for increasing events, Gauge for values that rise and fall, Histogram for distributions
Counter, Gauge and Summary for distributions
Counter, Gauge and Timer for wall clock"
monitoring.explanation: Counters only increase and suit rates like http_requests_total. Gauges move both ways and represent state such as queue depth. Histograms bucket observations so you can compute quantiles and rates of buckets, and unlike Summaries they aggregate correctly across instances, which is why Histogram is the default choice.

monitoring.text: What do the RED and USE frameworks measure?
options: RED covers request rate, errors and duration for services; USE covers utilisation, saturation and errors for resources
RED is for databases and USE is for HTTP
They measure the same things in different orders
USE is the newer name for RED"
monitoring.explanation: RED is the user-facing service view and USE is the constrained-resource view. Saturation is the interesting part of USE because utilisation can be high and fine right up until queues build, which is where latency actually degrades.

monitoring.text: What is the most direct fix for a Prometheus instance exhausting memory due to ingest?
options: Drop high-cardinality labels such as user_id or request_id
Increase the scrape interval to five minutes
monitoring.explanation: Prometheus stores a series per unique label combination, so an unbounded label multiplies series count and is the usual cause of high memory and slow queries. Drop it from metrics and route that dimension to logs or traces instead. More replicas do not reduce per-replica memory.

monitoring.text: What is an SLO error budget and how should it guide decisions?
options: The permitted unreliability, which you may spend on releases; exhausting it means prioritising reliability
A fixed monetary budget for the observability stack
The number of alerts allowed per week
monitoring.explanation: An error budget of 0.1% on a 99.9% SLO is the unreliability available to spend. While budget remains, shipping features is correct; once exhausted, reliability work takes priority. This replaces the 'move fast versus move carefully' argument with an objective number.

monitoring.text: What makes an alert actionable rather than noise?
options: A clear owner, a user-impact or SLO-burn threshold, and a runbook link
Alerting on every warning log line
monitoring.explanation: An actionable alert names what is broken for users, who owns it and what to do. Page on symptoms and burn rate rather than causes, because cause-based alerts fire for things not yet hurting anyone. Runbook links and a routing policy are what separate a page from a notification.

monitoring.text: What are the four golden signals?
options: Availability, durability, consistency and partition tolerance
Mean, median, mode and standard deviation"
monitoring.explanation: From the Google SRE book, these four generalise across services, queues and databases, which is why they work as a starting point before you tailor RED or USE to a specific system. Saturation is the one most often omitted and most predictive of future pain.

monitoring.text: Why does a high-cardinality alert threshold matter for Prometheus?
options: An unbounded label can grow series count until queries and memory degrade
monitoring.explanation: A metric with user_id or request_id creates a new series per value, and Prometheus holds all of them in memory. Beyond a threshold the whole instance degrades, so cardinality budgets and label allowlists are an operational necessity rather than an optimisation.

monitoring.text: What does a burn-rate alert on an SLO do differently from alerting on raw error percentage?
options: It alerts on how fast the error budget is being consumed, which correlates with user pain
It requires a longer evaluation window
It only works with multi-window alerts"
monitoring.explanation: Burn rate alerts use multi-window, multi-burn-rate configurations so they fire fast when consumption is rapid and stay quiet for slow burns that would otherwise cause alert fatigue. Raw error percentage has no notion of how much budget exists, so the same number means different things for a 99% and a 99.99% SLO.

monitoring.text: What is the difference between a counter-based rate and a gauge-based average for request rate?
options: Rates from counters are correct across resets and scaling; averaging a gauge can hide or distort the rate
Gauges cannot be used for rate calculations
monitoring.explanation: A rate over a counter is computed as the increase over a window divided by the window, which handles counter resets and instance scaling correctly. Averaging a per-instance gauge over instances weights by instance count rather than traffic, so a busy and an idle instance are treated equally, which is wrong.

monitoring.text: Why is log volume often the largest cost driver in an observability stack?
options: Logs are unstructured and high-volume, with retention usually far longer than metrics
Logs are more expensive to index than traces
monitoring.explanation: Logs dwarf metrics and traces in volume, are expensive to index, and are commonly retained far longer, which makes them the first thing to reduce through sampling, filtering at collection, and moving to cheaper archive storage. Cardinality matters in logs too, since every unique label multiplies stored series.

monitoring.text: What does trace sampling in a distributed system typically cost you?
options: You lose visibility into the errors you did not sample, so error-biased sampling is usually preferable
monitoring.explanation: Head-based sampling keeps a fixed percentage and can easily drop the one trace that explains an intermittent failure. Tail-based sampling buffers and decides per complete trace, which lets you keep all errors and slow traces while discarding boring successes, at the cost of added buffer latency.

monitoring.text: What is the purpose of a runbook linked from an alert?
options: It tells the on-call engineer what the alert means and what to do, reducing time to mitigate
monitoring.explanation: A runbook converts a page into action: what broke, how to confirm it, the safe mitigation, and when to escalate. Without one, the responder spends the incident's most expensive minutes searching. Runbooks should be tested, since an untested one is worse than none.

monitoring.text: What distinguishes a percentile from a mean when describing latency?
options: A percentile describes a tail experienced by some users; a mean can look healthy while the tail is terrible
Percentiles are always larger than means
They are the same when data is uniform"
monitoring.explanation: A mean can be dominated by the bulk of fast requests and stay flat while a small, very slow group suffers, which is exactly the group that tweets at you. Track p50, p95 and p99 separately, and remember percentiles cannot be averaged across instances, which is why histograms rather than Summaries are used.

monitoring.text: Why is a percentile better than an average when measuring request latency?
options: Averages hide the slow tail that real users actually experience
Percentiles cannot be aggregated across services
monitoring.explanation: If 1% of requests take 30 seconds, the average barely moves but a meaningful number of users had a bad time. p50, p95 and p99 describe the experience; the average does not.

monitoring.text: What does a high p99 with a normal p50 usually indicate?
options: A small number of very slow requests, often GC pauses, lock contention or a slow dependency
monitoring.explanation: The gap between median and tail is the signature of intermittent problems: garbage collection pauses, connection pool exhaustion or a downstream call occasionally hanging. Uniform slowness shows up in p50 too.

monitoring.text: When should an alert fire on a symptom rather than a cause?
options: When the symptom is user-visible and you want fewer, more actionable pages
Always, because causes are more specific
monitoring.explanation: Alerting on CPU causes pages nobody can act on. Alerting on error rate and latency pages the team that can fix it. Causes belong on a dashboard for diagnosis, not in the paging path.

monitoring.text: What makes an alert actionable that a dashboard notification is not?
options: It has a runbook link, a clear owner, and fires on something a human must act on now
monitoring.explanation: An alert is an interruption. That cost is only justified if there is a named owner, a documented response, and a reason to act immediately. Everything else belongs on a dashboard people check.

monitoring.text: What does cardinality mean for a metric label?
options: The number of distinct values a label takes, which multiplies storage and query cost
The time range of a query
monitoring.explanation: Labelling every metric with a user ID creates millions of time series from one metric, which is a common and expensive self-inflicted outage. Keep labels to bounded values like status code or endpoint.

monitoring.text: Why is a scrape-based monitoring system a poor fit for very short-lived containers?
options: The container may exit before it is ever scraped
It only works with virtual machines
monitoring.explanation: A pod that lives 200 milliseconds may never exist at a scrape instant. For that, push metrics from a sidecar or agent, or use the orchestrator's own event stream.

monitoring.text: What is the main operational risk of relying solely on a shallow metrics-based health check?
options: A service can serve errors quickly and still be reported healthy
monitoring.explanation: Liveness checks that only verify the process responds will happily keep a service in rotation while it returns 500s. Readiness and startup probes should check what the service actually depends on.

monitoring.text: What does a distributed trace give you that metrics and logs do not?
options: The causal path across services for a single request, with per-span timing
A count of errors per endpoint
A single dashboard for all services
monitoring.explanation: Metrics tell you something is slow; traces tell you which hop is responsible. Sampling keeps the volume manageable while preserving the ability to inspect an individual slow request.

monitoring.text: What is the purpose of log levels, and what is a common misuse?
options: They filter noise; the misuse is leaving debug enabled in production, which floods storage and hides real errors
monitoring.explanation: Levels exist so operators can raise or lower verbosity without a deploy. Leaving debug on in production is the standard failure: it fills the pipeline, raises cost, and pushes important lines out of retention.

monitoring.text: How should you measure an SLO rather than a metric?
options: As the proportion of good events to valid events over a window, with an error budget derived from it
As an absolute threshold on one service
As the number of alerts per week
monitoring.explanation: An SLO is a user-facing reliability target over a period. The error budget that falls out of it is what tells you whether you can ship a risky change this week or must spend the week on stability.

monitoring.text: What causes alert fatigue and how is it best prevented?
options: Too many low-value alerts; fix it by requiring an owner and a runbook, and deleting alerts nobody acts on
monitoring.explanation: People stop reading alerts when most are noise, and then miss the real one. Auditing which alerts have ever produced a response is the fastest way to cut the volume.

monitoring.text: What does a histogram bucket boundary change affect?
options: The accuracy of percentile estimates for values in that range
monitoring.explanation: Latency is a distribution, and percentiles are computed from buckets. Moving boundaries around the region you care about, typically the slow tail, changes how precisely p99 can be estimated there.

monitoring.text: Why should a service expose separate liveness and readiness probes?
options: Liveness answers should it be restarted; readiness answers should it receive traffic. Conflating them causes restart storms
It halves the number of probes
Readiness probes are required by Kubernetes
monitoring.explanation: If readiness returns failure whenever a dependency blips, every instance leaves the load balancer at once and the outage spreads. Liveness should stay shallow so a slow dependency does not trigger a restart loop.

monitoring.text: What is the main drawback of using host-level CPU as a scaling signal?
options: CPU is a poor proxy for demand and can lag or mislead under IO-bound work
CPU is too expensive to collect
It cannot be collected per pod
It only works in the cloud
monitoring.explanation: IO-bound services often sit at low CPU while queue depth climbs, so autoscaling on CPU under-provisions them. Queue length or request concurrency tracks demand more directly for those workloads.

networking.text: In what order does a typical HTTPS request resolve and connect?
options: DNS, then TCP, then TLS, then HTTP
TCP, then DNS, then TLS, then HTTP
TLS, then DNS, then TCP, then HTTP
DNS, then HTTP, then TLS, then TCP"
networking.explanation: The client resolves the name, establishes TCP with a three-way handshake, negotiates TLS, and only then sends the HTTP request. Each step is a place latency accrues, which is why connection reuse and session resumption matter. HTTP/3 over QUIC folds transport and TLS together but still needs an address first.

networking.text: What does a DNS TTL control?
options: How long resolvers may cache the record, which bounds how fast a change propagates
The lifetime of the DNS server process
How long a TLS certificate is cached
networking.explanation: TTL sets the cache lifetime, so a high TTL slows failover and a low one speeds it at the cost of more queries. Some resolvers and ISPs ignore short TTLs and cache longer, so failover time is a floor rather than a guarantee, and client-side caches are separate again.

networking.text: What is the three-way TCP handshake?
options: SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK, requiring a full round trip before data flows
SYN then data, with no acknowledgement
networking.explanation: The client sends SYN, the server replies SYN-ACK, the client sends ACK, and only then can data flow. That is one full round trip before the first byte of the request, so every additional hop adds real latency and connection reuse matters proportionally more on long paths.

networking.text: How many usable host addresses does a /28 provide in an AWS VPC?
networking.explanation: A /28 leaves 4 host bits, giving 16 addresses, and AWS reserves all five of the first and last: network address, the VPC router, DNS at .2, future use, and broadcast. On a traditional network only two are reserved, giving 14, and this asymmetry catches people out in VPC design.

networking.text: What is MTU and how does it relate to a common packet-drop problem?
options: MTU is the largest frame an interface sends; encapsulation overhead can exceed the path MTU and cause silent drops
MTU is the number of concurrent connections
MTU is the timeout before a packet is retried
networking.explanation: MTU is 1500 on Ethernet; MSS is MTU minus headers, roughly 1460 for IPv4. Tunnels and overlays add headers, and if the result exceeds the path MTU with Don't Fragment set, routers drop it silently. The symptom is a connection that works for small requests and hangs on large ones; the fix is clamping MSS or lowering the interface MTU.

networking.text: What does a layer 4 load balancer do that a layer 7 one cannot?
options: Forward by port while preserving the client IP, with less protocol parsing and lower latency
networking.explanation: An L4 balancer moves packets by port, so it preserves the source address and handles very high throughput, but it cannot inspect HTTP. An L7 balancer can route by path or header and terminate TLS, at the cost of more CPU and latency.

networking.text: What is connection tracking and why does exhausting it break services?
options: The kernel tracks flow state; a full table drops new connections, often after a scan or spike
It balances new connections across backends
networking.explanation: conntrack holds an entry per flow across the firewall. When the table fills, the kernel refuses to create new entries, presenting as random connection failures under load. Raising nf_conntrack_max and the buckets is the direct fix, and it is a common cause of mysterious intermittent failures on NAT or load-balancer instances.

networking.text: Why does asymmetric routing break stateful firewalls?
options: Return traffic takes a different path, so the firewall has no state for the flow
The firewall cannot handle high throughput
Asymmetric routes are blocked by BGP
networking.explanation: A stateful firewall expects both directions of a flow through the same device. If replies return via another router, the firewall sees them as unsolicited inbound and drops them. This is a classic multi-AZ pitfall when routing is not designed symmetrically.

networking.text: Which DNS record type maps a hostname directly to an IPv6 address?
networking.explanation: AAAA is the IPv6 equivalent of A. A CNAME aliases one name to another and cannot coexist with other record types at the same name, which is why the zone apex cannot be a CNAME. PTR is the reverse lookup record.

networking.text: What does DNSSEC provide that a TLS certificate does not?
options: Authenticated DNS data, preventing record tampering in transit
networking.explanation: DNSSEC signs DNS records so a validating resolver can detect tampering, but it does not encrypt queries and it is not confidentiality. TLS on the connection is what protects the data; DNSSEC protects the name resolution step.

networking.text: What causes a slow TLS handshake to be much worse for mobile clients than for a datacentre client?
options: Higher and more variable round-trip time, and per-connection session setup cost
Mobile devices use older ciphers by default
Handshakes are cached only on wifi"
networking.explanation: Handshake cost is dominated by round trips, so latency multiplies it. TLS 1.3 with session resumption cuts this to roughly one round trip, and 0-RTT or connection coalescing cuts it further. Without resumption, a high-latency mobile client pays the full cost on every new connection.

networking.text: Why can a route flap between availability zones cause application-level failures even when connectivity looks fine?
options: Each shift can reset in-flight TCP connections and shift traffic to unequal or degraded targets
Flapping is a layer 2 problem only
networking.explanation: Route flapping means traffic repeatedly shifts paths, and every shift can break in-flight TCP connections, remap clients onto cold caches, and create uneven load. It is often a symptom of asymmetric routing, which also breaks conntrack, so the two problems frequently appear together.

networking.text: What is the effect of a lower DNS TTL before a planned migration?
options: Resolvers re-query sooner, so the change propagates faster at the cost of more queries
It has no effect until a restart
It only affects the primary nameserver
networking.explanation: Lower the TTL well before you need to move traffic, and raise it again afterwards to reduce query volume. Remember some resolvers and ISPs cache longer than the TTL, and client-side caches add their own delay, so this shortens the window without eliminating it.

networking.text: Which problem does HTTP/3 over QUIC specifically address?
options: Head-of-line blocking across streams at the transport layer, and loss of packets affecting unrelated streams
networking.explanation: HTTP/2 fixed application-layer head-of-line blocking but kept it at the transport layer, where a lost TCP packet stalls every stream. QUIC runs over UDP with independent streams and per-stream loss recovery, so one lost packet does not block the others. It also allows 0-RTT resumption.

networking.text: What does an anycast address do?
options: Advertises the same address from multiple locations so traffic goes to the nearest
Assigns a unique address per client
networking.explanation: Anycast advertises one IP from many sites, and normal routing sends traffic to the closest, which is how DNS root servers and CDNs work. Unlike L4 load balancing, it has no awareness of connection state, so TCP connection migration requires QUIC.

networking.text: Why can a CNAME record not be placed at the apex of a DNS zone?
options: A CNAME cannot coexist with any other record type at the same name, and the apex requires SOA and NS
APEX records are not supported by any resolver
A CNAME must be a subdomain
networking.explanation: The apex must carry SOA and NS records, and a CNAME cannot be combined with any other data at the same name. Providers work around this with ALIAS or ANAME records that resolve server-side, which is why apex CNAMEs often appear to work through a hosting provider but not on plain DNS.

networking.text: What is a common cause of intermittent TLS handshake failures only on some mobile networks?
options: An incomplete certificate chain that clients cannot fetch because AIA fetching is blocked
The record has a low TTL"
networking.explanation: A server must send the leaf plus the intermediates needed to build a path, and should omit the root. If the intermediate is missing and the client cannot fetch it because access to the CA's URL is blocked, validation fails with no obvious error. Carrier networks commonly block such fetches.

networking.text: What does the SNI extension solve?
options: Allows multiple TLS certificates to be served from one IP by including the requested hostname in the handshake
networking.explanation: Without SNI, a client sends only an IP address, so a shared IP cannot know which certificate to present. SNI carries the hostname in the ClientHello. Its limitation is that it is not encrypted by default, which is what Encrypted Client Hello addresses.

networking.text: Which two ranges cover all subnets in a 10.0.0.0/16 VPC CIDR?
networking.explanation: A /16 fixes the first 16 bits and lets the rest vary, giving 10.0.0.0 through 10.0.255.255. Reference the broad VPC CIDR in peering and gateway routes, but narrow subnet CIDRs in security groups, so that a wide rule does not quietly cover more than intended.

networking.text: What is the role of a NAT gateway in a VPC?
options: Translates private addresses to a public address so outbound traffic can return
networking.explanation: NAT rewrites private sources to the gateway's Elastic IP and translates back on return traffic, using a port mapping table. Private subnets deliberately have no route to the internet gateway, so outbound needs a NAT gateway; inbound needs a public subnet with an Elastic IP or a load balancer in front of private targets.

networking.text: Why does traceroute showing hops beyond the failure point not mean the problem is there?
options: Routers deprioritise ICMP TTL-exceeded responses, so hop N+3 may simply not reply
Those hops are in the destination region
networking.explanation: When a router decrements the TTL to zero it sends an ICMP time-exceeded message, and generating that message is low priority. So a hop that fails to respond is not necessarily the hop that dropped the traffic. Look for the first hop from which probes stop being received entirely, and corroborate with MTR loss patterns rather than a single traceroute run.

networking.text: What does MTR give you that a single traceroute does not?
options: Continuous per-hop statistics over time, so loss patterns are visible rather than inferred
networking.explanation: MTR sends repeated probes and aggregates loss and latency per hop over a window, which distinguishes an intermittent drop from a hop that simply does not reply to ICMP. That distinction is exactly what a single traceroute run cannot make.

networking.text: What is the effect of enabling TCP keepalive without also configuring idle timeouts sensibly?
options: Connections can be reaped by a middlebox while both endpoints believe them open, causing silent stalls
It forces HTTPS on all connections"
networking.explanation: Middleboxes drop idle connections, but the endpoints still consider them established. The first write after the gap stalls until a keepalive detects it. Either enable TCP keepalive with sensible intervals, or make the application-level idle timeout shorter than any middlebox's, which is why load balancers' keep-alive settings matter so much.

networking.text: Why does a 502 from a load balancer specifically rule out client-side DNS?
options: The load balancer generated it, which means the request already reached the load balancer
DNS is never involved in HTTP
The client would show a different code
502 is defined as a DNS error"
networking.explanation: A 502 is produced by the load balancer after accepting the TCP connection but failing to get a valid HTTP response from a target, so the client's name resolution and connectivity to the load balancer both demonstrably worked. A 503 means no healthy targets, a 504 a timeout. Establishing that first saves an hour of looking in the wrong place.

terraform.text: What does terraform plan show you that terraform apply then performs?
options: A proposed diff of create, update, destroy and replace actions
The exact API calls that will be made
A validation of HCL syntax only
The current state of every resource"
terraform.explanation: plan compares configuration, state and reality and reports the actions required. It does not show the exact API calls, which is why an apply can still fail on something outside Terraform's control such as a quota or a permissions change.

terraform.text: Why must remote state be stored with encryption and locking?
options: State holds plaintext secrets and concurrent applies can corrupt it
Remote state is slower than local state
terraform.explanation: Providers persist every attribute into state, including passwords and tokens. Locking prevents two engineers applying at once and overwriting each other's view of reality. Neither is optional for a shared backend.

terraform.text: What does the '# forces replacement' marker in a plan mean?
options: Changing that attribute cannot be done in place, so the resource will be destroyed and recreated
The resource will be updated in place
The plan cannot proceed without input
The provider version is too old"
terraform.explanation: Some attributes are immutable after creation, such as an EC2 instance's subnet or an EBS volume's Availability Zone. Replacement risks downtime and can orphan a public IP or an Elastic IP, so treat those lines as breaking changes.

terraform.text: What is the difference between count and for_each on a resource?
options: count takes a number and indexes from zero; for_each takes a set or map and keys by value, which is stable
count supports maps, for_each does not"
terraform.explanation: count's keys are positional, so removing an item from the middle of a list shifts every later index and forces replacement. for_each keys by the given key, so removing one item affects only that instance. Prefer for_each whenever the keys are meaningful.

terraform.text: What does the sensitive attribute on a resource actually do?
options: Redacts the value in CLI output; the value is still written to state and plan files in plaintext
Prevents the value from being sent to the provider
terraform.explanation: The flag only suppresses display. The value persists in state and in saved plan output, so the real fix is keeping secrets out of Terraform entirely and injecting them at runtime from Secrets Manager or SSM. Marking a resource sensitive also just makes it harder to debug.

terraform.text: When should you use terraform state mv?
options: After refactoring module structure, to re-point state at the same real resource
To move a resource between AWS accounts
To migrate a resource between regions
terraform.explanation: state mv updates the state mapping without destroying or recreating anything, which is exactly what you need after reorganising modules. state rm forgets a resource so Terraform stops managing it. Never hand-edit state.

terraform.text: What is Terraform drift, and what is the right response?
options: Real resources changed outside Terraform; investigate the cause before applying, since apply would revert the change
terraform.explanation: During an incident someone fixes something in the console, and the next plan wants to revert it. Applying blindly would undo the fix, so find out who changed what and why, then either import the change or bring the code in line.

terraform.text: What does create_before_destroy do, and when is it required?
options: Creates the replacement before destroying the original, required when two of the same resource cannot coexist
Creates resources in a different region
Prevents the resource from being destroyed"
terraform.explanation: Needed for resources that cannot overlap, such as a security group on an ENI, a database with a fixed name, or a DNS record with the same name. It is often paired with a unique name and sometimes a depends_on to force ordering.

terraform.text: Why pin provider versions with required_providers?
options: To keep configuration reproducible and avoid a provider upgrade turning a green apply red
To prevent providers making API calls
terraform.explanation: Without a version constraint, init can pull a provider with breaking behaviour. Commit the lock file so local, CI and production resolve identically, and let Renovate or Dependabot bump versions on a schedule.

terraform.text: What happens when a module variable has no default and the caller does not set it?
options: Terraform prompts interactively, or errors in automation
It defaults to null and the resource is skipped
terraform.explanation: A variable without a default is required. In a terminal Terraform prompts; in CI there is no terminal, so it fails with a clear message. Always add type constraints too, since they catch wrong values at validate time rather than apply time.

terraform.text: What is the recommended pattern for sharing one S3 backend across many small configurations?
options: One state key per configuration, isolated by path, with locking enabled
A single shared state key for all of them
Local state committed to a private repo
A separate AWS account per configuration with no backend"
terraform.explanation: Each configuration needs its own state, achieved with distinct keys or Terraform Cloud workspaces. Sharing one key causes conflicting writes and lock contention, which is a genuinely painful failure to debug.

terraform.text: What does a lifecycle ignore_changes block do?
options: Tells Terraform to stop detecting drift on the listed attributes
Forces the resource to be replaced
terraform.explanation: ignore_changes suppresses drift detection for the listed attributes so Terraform leaves them alone. It is appropriate when something else legitimately owns the attribute, such as a default VPC setting or a tag mutated by an autoscaler, but it is also the easy way to hide a real bug, so use it deliberately.

terraform.text: What does terraform validate do?
options: Checks configuration syntax and internal consistency without contacting providers
terraform.explanation: validate catches type errors, bad references and invalid argument shapes locally, with no API calls, so it is fast and belongs in a pre-commit or CI step. It will not catch things that only surface against real infrastructure, which is why plan matters too.

terraform.text: Why is it a problem to hardcode a value that also exists as a computed attribute?
options: It becomes a permanent diff because Terraform tries to correct the value every plan
It causes the apply to fail
terraform.explanation: If you set an attribute the provider computes, every plan shows a change from the real value to your literal. The fix is to omit the argument and let it be computed, or to reference the resource attribute rather than hardcoding it.

terraform.text: What does the depends_on meta-argument control?
options: Explicit ordering between resources that have no implicit dependency through references
Whether a resource is created or destroyed
The order in which variables are evaluated"
terraform.explanation: Terraform infers ordering from references, which is nearly always what you want. depends_on is for the cases with no reference relationship, such as forcing an IAM policy attachment before a role is assumed. It over-couples resources, so reach for it only when necessary.

terraform.text: What is the difference between a count-indexed resource address and a for_each-keyed one, in terms of state?
options: Count addresses are positional, so reordering forces replacement; for_each addresses are stable across changes
for_each cannot be used with modules
Count addresses are stored in a separate file"
terraform.explanation: The address is how Terraform identifies a resource instance in state. Positional addresses mean a list edit is a destroy and create; keyed addresses mean only the changed key is touched. This is the single biggest source of accidental replacements.

terraform.text: Which command is appropriate for importing existing infrastructure into Terraform management?
options: terraform import, or an import block, which previews then applies
terraform.explanation: terraform import brings one existing resource under management; an import block does the same inside configuration, running plan first so you can see what it would do. Hand-editing state to add a resource is not supported.

terraform.text: What does a module output actually do?
options: Exposes a value from the child module to the caller
Writes a value to a file
Declares a variable with a default"
terraform.explanation: Outputs are the module's public interface, and a module without outputs is unusable to its caller. Marking an output sensitive keeps it out of plan output but, as with resources, the value is still in state.

terraform.text: What is the effect of a remote state backend with a DynamoDB or S3 lock table?
options: It serialises applies so two runs cannot corrupt each other's state
terraform.explanation: Locking is about concurrency: without it, two applies can both read the same state and the second write loses the first's changes. Encryption is configured separately with server-side encryption on the bucket.

terraform.text: Why should base images be pinned by digest rather than tag in an infrastructure pipeline?
options: Tags are mutable, so two builds of the same commit can differ
Tags cannot be used with caching
